utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Dr. Rudolf. Welcome again. May we remind you of the affirmation you took at the commencement of the proceedings. Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, when we broke last time, we were looking at some documents under -- that had been at tab 9 of the binders. Sorry, not tab 9. I'm so sorry. I'll get it for you in a second. Tab 13. There were several sets of documents. And the first of them we had begun to look at, I believe the document which has been labelled P165, which discussed information about the lives of the negotiators - yourself, Mr. Cifric, and Mr. Kriste - being at risk. Moving on to additional documents in that section, I would ask that the document labelled -- that bears the ERN -- in English, it's 03091853; in Serbo-Croatian, it's 01076134 -- be shown to you, please. If it would make it easier, I can also ask that the next set of documents, to save some steps for Mr. Usher, which would be English 03091852, Croatian 01076133 also be shown. And 01 -- and English 03091854 Serbo-Croatian, 01076135. So there are basically three sets of documents that will be presented to you for your speedy review. Mr. Rudolf, do you have in front of you the document which is dated the 7th of December and it -- in the upper corner, 01076134 in Serbo-Croatian, shows 1015 hours. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just indicate, please -- I will run through it for you, and ask, first of all, do you recognise this particular document?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And is it a document that came from your hand, whether it was authored by you?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is on Dubrovnik Coastal Radio Station, and it is a request to transmit the following message to the Boka Naval Sector Command, to Vice Admiral Miodrag Jokic: "Reference: Our radio telegram of this morning. Because of damage which we have just determined that the vessel Arka has suffered, we are forced to replace it with the vessel Krila Dubrovnika with respect to which we hereby ask you that you assure its free and safe passage under UNICEF's flag from Gruz harbour via the south side of the island of Lokrum to Cavtat, that is, to your ship and back." Now, did you, in fact, depart on that vessel? Is this correct? Does this represent the means by which you would leave from Dubrovnik to Cavtat for completion of the negotiations, on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, if you would turn, please, to the next document, which is in English the 03091852; in Serbo-Croatian, 01076133. Do you see that, Mr. Rudolf?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat the numbers. 617891?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is the very first -- it's actually a single document, Mr. Rudolf. It's in Serbo-Croatian, 01076133. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: 61 -- yes, I see it. It's on the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the tab number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It's all from 13, Your Honour. There were several documents under tab 13. And it was -- has the Chamber been able to find it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The text of it, it is for yourself. Do you recognise this document? Do you recognise the text of it?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is from the Boka Naval Sector, dated 7 December at 1110 hours, address to you, the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff for Minister Davorin Rudolf. "We accept your suggestion that you travel aboard the Krila Dubrovnika hydrofoil boat. There is a gale in Cavtat so it will be difficult to hold talks. We suggest that you sail into Srebreno harbour where we will be waiting for you to hold talks. Will assure the safety of your vessel from Srebreno harbour and back, and your own personal safety." Did you, upon receipt of this, set sail? I'm sorry, Mr. Rudolf, on receipt of this communication --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And again, the confirmation of that is the next document, which in English is 03091854; Serbo-Croatian, 01076135. Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Rudolf?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is dated 7th of December. It is to Admiral Jokic, Boka Naval Sector. In Serbo-Croatian it shows an 1130 hour. "With reference to your radio telegram received at 1100 --" or I have 1110 pencilled in -- "we confirm our arrival in Srebreno." Signed Davorin Rudolf. Does this succinctly show the order of communiques that preceded your departure with the assurances you needed to go and conduct he negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I ask to move all three documents into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears these documents are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do not have numbers on these particular documents, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think that was a different one, from tab 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: P165 is dated the 7th of December, but it is a different document. It's the English of number 57, 1857. But not the other ones, it seems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So there are three documents, Madam Registrar, one of which is the first one, which ends, in English, 1853, in Serbo-Croatian, 6134. We ask for --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That one would be marked as P168.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The second one would be, if I may assist you, it ends in, in English, 1852, in Serbo-Croatian, 6133.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked P169.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the last was ending in -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 1854, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. And in Serbo-Croatian 6135.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, when you set from Dubrovnik, did you in fact land in Srebreno? Did you dock in Srebreno?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes we came to the Srebreno port. However, this hydrofoil had very deep paws, and we couldn't set in, we couldn't berth in. We threw the rope, admiral Jokic grabbed it and tried to tie it, but we couldn't get close to the shore because the hydrofoil had these deep paws, and we agreed therefore to go to Cavtat instead and carry out our negotiations there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You said that Admiral Jokic grabbed the rope or the line for the boat. Where was Admiral Jokic when you arrived at Srebreno?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't set in. We couldn't berth in because there was this very high breakwater.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right. Where was Admiral Jokic then? Was he actually waiting for you at the dock? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the dock itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did he personally take the line and try to tie the line of the boat, the rope of the boat?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you were not able to dock in Srebreno, what did you then do? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We agreed that we should go to Cavtat to hold negotiations there. That's what we did. We went there by boat, and I believe that Admiral Jokic took the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, in Cavtat, we have gone over earlier the various provisions of the signed series of negotiations. I will just ask, if I can ask Madam Case Manager just to direct me to the exhibit number or the tab, if possible. If not, I'll look quickly. My question to you, though, is there were a number of points in the cease-fire -- in the comprehensive negotiation agreement that you signed on the 7th of December. Did Admiral Jokic offer any resistance to any of the provisions in that agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is on page -- tab 14 of your binders, if it would be of any help.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there any resistance or was there agreement on the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He offered no resistance. He had only two objections, only two comments. One was that all the obligations were on the army's side because -- and we had no obligations at all. And his second comment was that we wrote the text in Croatian whereas he said that it would be good to have it in Serbian, so we made a compromise. In some places we used the name of the month in Croatian; in other places, we would write it in Serbian. Those were the only small details that had no particular importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was -- can you describe the -- shall we say the mood of the negotiating parties at that time, if you're able to comment.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations started with my protest on behalf of the Croatian government against the attack on Dubrovnik, whereupon Admiral Jokic got up, took the floor, and apologised for the attacks. He said that the Minister of Defence, General Kadijevic, will address an apology to me, Dubrovnik, and the European monitors. After that, I sat down, and then a representative of the European Community observers made a protest on behalf of the European observers. After that, Admiral Jokic responded once again and apologised, and then we started negotiating on the various items and started writing the text of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I want to be sure that I understand you correctly. The behaviour you described just now as an apology by Admiral Jokic, this was above and beyond the regret expressed in his faxed communication to you on the 6th of December? This is yet another apology at the time, on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I'm sorry, I just failed to mention that when we found ourselves in Cavtat, he gave me an envelope with a letter from General Strugar. In answer to your question, yes, he apologised again after expressing regret in his earlier radiogram and on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall if the monitors from the European Community were also -- were present at this time during these negotiations on the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was Mr. Hvalkof present with you inside?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was him. He was the one who stood up and expressed the protest on behalf of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At any time during negotiations on the 7th of December, did Admiral Jokic ever tell you that the forces of the JNA were trying to hit military targets or objectives inside the Old Town of Dubrovnik on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Since December 1991, have you had any contact with Admiral Jokic? Up to today's date; have you had any contact since then up until now?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just a second. I want to check one note. I would ask that the video from Witness Grbic, which is P66, which has an accompanying transcript, be shown through Sanction, and just for two or three points in there. I would ask also that the transcripts be distributed. We have them both in English and Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, I'm going to ask my colleague to show a part of a video which depicts a concert that is taking place in Dubrovnik, and then a news flash, as it were. It was, I believe, a televised concert. If we could just take a look at it, and I would direct the attention of those who have the transcripts in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We will advance it to the correct...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry, our -- thank you very much. What is in the background, as you can see, is -- appears to be a concert.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you see the date of 5 December 1991? Sorry, you should have heard music. You heard something over it. Are you able to read the byline which is underneath, the printing which is underneath? I'll ask my colleague to perhaps replay it so you can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, were you able to read the print as it was going past the screen? Are you familiar with that transmission or are you able to indicate whether or not this type of transmission -- first of all, would you be kind enough to tell the Chamber what it actually says. It should be on page --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In English, Your Honour, on page 13 of 20 in your English translation. It says "information ticker," 5/12/91.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says that in the occupied town of Cavtat, an agreement was reached with the Yugoslav People's Army on the strict observation of the cease-fire and that a concert was held in Dubrovnik to mark the anniversary of Mozart's death.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is this transmission or type of transmission shown to the public at large in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the fact of the negotiations known to the people of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely. It was our message and my message, because we considered that we had reached an oral, verbal agreement on the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the same video, moving ahead to portion -- let's see. The English would be the bottom of page 13, if I can ask Ms. McCreath to try to advance it. It discusses Major General Radomir Damjanovic is the text in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you can stop for a minute. The translation of that, Your Honours, is on page 13 at the bottom, continuing on to the top of page 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, the comment that is attributed to General Damjanovic, first of all, had you heard of General Damjanovic? Were you aware of who he may have been, who he was?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him, but I did not know that he was a general and things like that. I have heard of him, but I don't know anything in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The comment which was attributed to him, that the smoke was probably most -- was probably -- "most probably caused by arson, adding that was most probably a case of tyres being set on fire." Is this type of comment one that you had become familiar with as a --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was familiar with that. But I did not know that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. General, as it says here, Damjanovic, but I thought that it was somebody else, another general in Belgrade who had said it, General Gvero. This statement of General Gvero was broadcast over the radio or on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on, on to page 15 of the English transcript, and I'm trying to find it for -- I believe in B/C/S, it would be on page 18. I hope that helps. If I could ask my colleague to try to play...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you able to hear from the announcer who was portrayed on the screen? Did that come through? If not, I can ask Ms. McCreath to replay it. Perhaps part of it didn't come through.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what -- again, it is attributed to General Damjanovic. That was: "It was carried out by one small unit only when they started suffering more and more casualties," said Damjanovic. "Several grenades were fired at the old city, not intending to hit the buildings occupied by the citizens, but in order to neutralise mortar positions." Does this explanation comport with what you observed directly, first-hand in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, I do not believe that these transcripts had been offered into evidence at the time the video was. And if I may offer them into evidence to assist the Chamber, I would ask to do so, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P171.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think the transcript reflected that the agreement at tab 14 is already Exhibit P61.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That was a separate line of inquiry. I was asking Mr. Rudolf about another aspect of the agreement. But I wanted to make sure that this particular set of transcripts came to the Chamber and that some of the explanations offered were in evidence. Excuse me just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Dubrovnik after the conclusion of these negotiations, Mr. Rudolf?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about ten days altogether. Perhaps seven or eight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And during the period in which you were in Dubrovnik, were you satisfied that the terms of the negotiations were being implemented, that the parties had, in fact, made a determination to implement them, both sides?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The agreement of the 7th of December, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the JNA left -- or do you know when the JNA left Dubrovnik all together, if you're able to give a general time period? If you are not, it is all right as well. Did its presence continue into 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the town of Dubrovnik? They were not in Dubrovnik at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The area. The area.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the area. I think they finally left in May. I'm not sure. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know whether or not General Strugar was still in theatre at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you say --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware as to whether or not the forces under the control of the JNA indeed did thin out and were withdrawn from areas close to the city of Dubrovnik from where they had been originally positioned at the time of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you receive any particular protests from either the Croatian side -- or from the Croatian side within the ten-day period that you remained in Dubrovnik about the terms of the December 7th negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain: I spent a total of about ten days there. So all this time I spent in Dubrovnik was about ten days. And as far as I can remember, no, there were not any protests.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The expression of regret, the apology as it were, and the demeanour of Admiral Jokic on the 7th of December, are you able to indicate if you viewed it as with force, with conviction? Was it, in your view, from what you saw, heard, dealt with at the time, was it communicated to you with conviction from Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions at this time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could I just have a moment, please, so that I can fix the lectern.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Rudolf. I'm Goran Rodic, attorney-at-law. And on behalf of the Defence, I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that during the examination-in-chief, you said that as minister of maritime affairs in the Croatian government, or rather you were in the Croatian government as minister for maritime affairs from July 1990 until August 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I don't know the exact dates, but approximately that was about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is the year when you became minister 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor in the period from the 2nd to the 6th of October 2003?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a statement, but I don't know if that is the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You gave the statement in Zagreb, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: One statement in Zagreb and one statement here in The Hague. But I don't know the exact time of either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This statement from October 2003, did you read it? Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, the last one. Well, I've forgotten when I was last in The Hague. I think it was about two months ago, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, just before giving evidence here, did you read this statement of yours from October, and did you make any corrections?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last one, yes, I did make some corrections in view of the translation. It seems to me that the English text is better than the text in Croatian. There were two corrections, I believe, that were of major importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read paragraph 4 to you of your statement from October 2003. You say: "I was appointed on July 1991 and remained in office until August 1992."

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a mistake. It is 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So the correct date would be?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: July 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since it is a question of two years, this was probably not a full term of the government that you served on. I just wanted to ask you one more thing. Since we understand each other, since we speak similar languages, could you please pause briefly before answering my question so the transcript could correctly reflect what is being said.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the government after the democratic elections in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What did you do after August 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: After August 1992, I was president of the State Commission for Borders. And after that, ambassador in Rome. I was actually accredited to Italy, Malta, San Marino.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, while you were minister for maritime affairs, the Prime Minister was Mr. Greguric. Right?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first Prime Minister was Stjepan Mesic, Mr. Stjepan Mesic. The second government had Mr. Manolic as its Prime Minister. And Mr. Greguric was Prime Minister of the third government. And I was a minister in all three of these governments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that only in 1993, if I'm not mistaken, you became an active member of the Croatian Democratic Union and that you were its member until 1999.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So in all these three previous governments in which you were minister, whose candidate were you?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was no one's candidate. And I did not belong to any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during your term of office as minister for maritime affairs from 1990 until 1992, did you attend government meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you attend some meetings with the then-president, Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was in charge of the government, yes. And for a while, I was minister of foreign affairs. Of course, I don't know what you mean by "meetings" actually, but when consultations were supposed to be held, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In addition to being minister for maritime affairs and minister of foreign affairs for a while, did you have any other position in the then-government or in any body that the government established at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The State Commission for Borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell me, at that time, was there a Supreme State Council?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who made up this council?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the president of the republic and a number of ministers. And of course, when I was minister for foreign affairs, then I was a member, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you took part in the meetings of the Supreme State Council on certain occasions?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know when the National Guards Corps was established in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think it was around the month of March 1991. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In that period, were the units of the National Guards Corps of the MUP of Croatia armed?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. How else would they operate? How else would there be such units?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these weapons imported?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know the origin, where the weapons came from?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they were seized from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you the following: In response to my previous question - the question was actually do you know where the weapons came from - what is the answer?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this was not within my line of work, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the answer that you gave to my other question, that weapons were obtained by being seized from the JNA, can you explain that to me in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was generally known. I'll tell you, I concluded an agreement with General Cado for the Rijeka area, and the JNA had to return the weapons of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia. Also, for this second agreement, the one that I concluded in Zitnic, it was agreed that the Yugoslav People's Army should return the weapons of the Territorial Defence. And I think that in both cases, the weapons were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That is governed by an agreement with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Then if -- in my opinion, that cannot be called seizing.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Call it what you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there any real seizure in the real sense of that word?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you are aware of the fate of some barracks where the JNA withdrew, leaving weapons behind, such as in Varazdin and some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In that period, 1991, were there any attacks as well on JNA barracks and units stationed in them?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not follow these events to be able to answer this precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this discussed at all at meetings of the government of Croatia? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to this now because any answer I could give would be neither precise nor accurate. But of course, our relations with the Yugoslav People's Army were discussed very often and at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you give me some details of those discussions that took place at government sessions regarding the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the objective of the Croatian government was to suppress, to avoid armed conflict, because Croatia did not have any weapons in the beginning, or did not have enough to resist such a powerful force as the Yugoslav People's Army, which was thought then to be the fourth strongest army in Europe. And many of our agreements were motivated by a desire to avoid conflict and reach a compromise. I remember government sessions where we would agree with General Raseta concerning some places around Zagreb on a cessation of hostilities, and then several hours later, or the next day, we would receive news that the Yugoslav People's Army entered those towns. You probably know that in places where clashes occur, especially between some rebelling insurgent Serbs and the Croatian forces, the Yugoslav People's Army would come, deploy, and support the insurgent Serbs. That happened in the Knin Krajina and in occupied territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, beginning with 1991, did you spend most of your time in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were JNA barracks besieged at the time? Did they have their electricity and amenities cut off?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe not to all of them, but to some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that that was -- is it the case that many of the barracks, the majority of the barracks suffered from blockade?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that. But I can tell you that the JNA supported insurgent Serbs in Croatia, and later supported the Serb policy in Croatia to the full. We in Croatia believed that had the JNA assumed a neutral position, many clashes and many conflicts could have been avoided. Why otherwise should we have requested the JNA to leave our territory, the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of the numbers of incidents involving attacks on barracks, military installations, and JNA units in the period from the beginning of 1991 to October that same year?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You wrote a book from which we received a couple of excerpts. It is titled "The War We Didn't Want." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me in which year the book was written.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it in 1997, 1998, and as you see, it was published in 1999. May I add that it was based on material from Belgrade sources, not Croatian sources, in order to be as authentic as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you use Croatian sources when you wrote the book, when you were writing the book?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but for the most part, what is most important comes from Belgrade sources; namely, diaries of the man who was then the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Mr. Jovic, a Serb; and the book written by General Kadijevic. Both these books were published in Belgrade. And you can see clearly from these books how the war was planned, how it was prepared, and who started it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you maybe present at a celebration of the anniversary of independence on the 24th of May 1992 at Ban Jelacic Square in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which independence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I mean the anniversary of the proclamation of independence.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: 24th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia proclaimed its independence on the 25th of June. I'm not familiar with the date that you quoted. Croatia proclaimed its independence on the 25th of June 1992 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. But when did you carry out the referendum?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that. But it doesn't matter. The referendum was only a preparatory step for the proclamation of independence. And that was on the same day as the Slovenian referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that Franjo Tudjman, at the ceremony to mark the anniversary of independence, stated that the war would never have taken place had the Croatians not wanted it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise, but I believe there may be a transcript error. The question was Croatia proclaimed its independence on the 25th of June, and it shows a date of 1992. That's not what I believe was heard. If it could be possibly redirected to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I discussed the date with the witness already, the 24th of May. My question is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the question was it proclaimed its independence on the 25th of June. And the transcript says 1992. I don't believe that's what the witness had indicated. And I wonder if it's possible just to rephrase the question and see if that is the answer he intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand what my learned friends means. Which answer? The 25th of June 1992; what's wrong with it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Rudolf, is the date upon which Croatia proclaimed its independence. Are you able to recall the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25th June 1991. That is the date when both Croatia and Slovenia proclaimed independence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There is also reference to a May 24th, and again the 1992 year came. It's off my screen. I just wonder if that might be re-inquired into because I don't think that's what was transmitted, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can't help with that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It's off my screen, and unfortunately -- perhaps my colleague could read it back. The page is page 20 and line 25. The question was: "What is the date of the proclamation of independence?" And the answer that was given was 24th of May 1992, and I wonder if that could be just re-inquired into, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've just got that as the 25th of June 1991. Could it have been the date of the anniversary of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It may well have been, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I've lost it. But if it has no significance to this witness, then I would just move on. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can move on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, is it true that President Tudjman, on the occasion of the anniversary of the independence of Croatia, the first anniversary in 1992, stated at Ban Jelacic Square: "The war would not have happened if Croatia had not wanted it? It was, however, our judgement that only through war can we achieve the independence of Croatia. That is why we conducted political negotiations, and behind those negotiations we set up military units. Had we not done so, we would never have reached our goal. That is to say, the war could have been avoided if only we had given up on our goals, that is, the independence of our state."

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that quotation. However, I lived there at the time, just as you lived in the other part, and I know that Croatia could not have started the war because it did not have the weapons to do so. That was the first precondition. Second, as you know, in the war that happened in Croatia, not a single Croatian soldier crossed over into the territory of either Serbia or Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That goes beyond the scope of my question.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You brought it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I brought up the quotation and asked you if you were familiar with those words. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That's what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, I suppose you are familiar with the status of the city of Dubrovnik which it enjoyed even in the times of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was Dubrovnik a demilitarised city?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it under the protection of UNESCO?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The Old Town of Dubrovnik was protected by UNESCO?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It continues to be protected by UNESCO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that a prerequisite for such a status was the demilitarisation of the entire Dubrovnik, including the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Dubrovnik was one of the four or five towns in Croatia that was proclaimed part of World Heritage, and as such, protected by UNESCO. I don't think demilitarisation was a prerequisite.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there was a JNA barracks in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you think that there could be weapons and military units in Dubrovnik despite the fact that the Old Town enjoys the status of a protected town, protected by UNESCO?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for instance, in 1987, 1988 - that is, before this war - were there any military assets in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But let me clarify one thing: When you say Dubrovnik, I understand you as meaning the entire city, not only the Old Town. And I do not know the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any JNA units in the city of Dubrovnik, which means the urban area of Dubrovnik, or maybe even the broader area of Dubrovnik? Were there any JNA units in the period before 1991?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before 1991, I don't know. But I suppose there were because it was the time when our state was Yugoslavia, and the Yugoslav People's Army was the army, and you know what the circumstances were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know when the ZNG, the National Guards Corps, was formed in Dubrovnik and when it began obtaining weapons along with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in July 1991 there began preparations for the defence of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, please, the following: You mentioned the role you played, namely, that the Croatian government gave you a mandate to negotiate with the General Cad in Rijeka and General Vukovic in Zitnic. Can you tell us, apart from these negotiations and the Dubrovnik negotiations you discussed earlier, did you play a role in any other negotiations with JNA representatives in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Split, with General Mladenic, we negotiated the withdrawal of JNA from Split in -- and Divulje. I believe I discussed with General Raseta their move to Rijeka and perhaps Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not quite clear about the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us about those negotiations that you mentioned and led as the minister for maritime affairs, were they closely linked to the coastal sector and this coastal belt of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it the reason why you were entrusted with this mandate because you are an expert for maritime affairs and the law of the sea?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it didn't have only to do with the sea itself. It also had to do with the islands and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the Rijeka Corps of the JNA, did it withdraw peacefully, without any violence or incidents?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was everything in accordance with the agreement that was reached?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this agreement preceded by some conflicts earlier on?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the negotiations with General Vladimir Vukovic, who was commander of the Knin Corps, you negotiated in Zitnic, didn't you? Tell me, was this agreement carried through?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in part, it was violated as well. It is the only agreement out of the three that was violated in the Zadar area, rather, in the hinterland of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was carried out, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know who negotiated with the JNA in other parts of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What did you know before you were given the mandate of the Croatian government, and to what extent were you familiar with the situation in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that in that area, conflicts had started, if I'm not mistaken, sometime in October in Konavle. I knew that Dubrovnik was blocked, which caused particular concern for us. I knew that the situation was very difficult down there and that my task was to reach a cease-fire agreement, first and foremost, and then to reach an agreement on the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information before you arrived in Dubrovnik as to how many agreements had been reached between the two sides, the Crisis Staff and the JNA, cease-fire agreements?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew, yes, that a series of such agreements had been reached, but that they were not observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you perhaps familiar with the proposal made by the JNA, it's called the 11-point agreement, that has to do with the normalisation of life in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. There were many proposals. But what was unacceptable in the talks that we had in Cavtat, too, was that Dubrovnik should be demilitarised, or rather, that Croatian armed forces should leave Dubrovnik. That was unacceptable because we did not trust the Yugoslav People's Army because they had violated such agreement. I already spoke about that when the lady was putting questions to me in relation to Cavtat. But there are other such examples. Many Croatian towns --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 8 of your statement, you say: "The local community had hitherto dealt with JNA in negotiations, and these negotiations were consistently failing due to lack of trust and breaches by possibly both sides."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Reading from the statement I think is an inappropriate way to ask a question. If there is a question, then perhaps there is a challenge to the statement, but that is not the format we have adopted in this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The concern, Mr. Rodic, is that you are simply reading slabs of the statement to the witness. You don't appear to be challenging that or querying it. As you know, there's a more appropriate way to be conducting your examination if you want to have the witness put into evidence something that's in his statement: Simply ignore the statement and go to the issue. Perhaps you could keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'm going to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, did both sides violate the numerous cease-fire agreements on the territory of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who exactly, but assumptions can be made. And that's the way I put it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection. It doesn't say violation of numerous cease-fire agreements. And at this point I would ask that counsel follow the evidence. The evidence was that cease-fire agreements had been entered into and that there were violations -- numerous cease-fire agreements, but there were violations. I don't recall that he said "numerous violations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know what you're getting at, Ms. Somers. We have just persuaded Mr. Rodic to put questions to the witness. He has put a question. He witness will either agree to it or not. Whether it accords with something said earlier is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this question was preceded by another one: Was the mandate of the witness to come to Dubrovnik to conclude a serious cease-fire agreement, because before that, several cease-fire agreements had been made and violated. And the witness said, while answering that previous question, that he was familiar with that. I simply wanted to make things clearer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who violated it and when, I really don't know. But generally speaking, agreements were not being observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, before you went to Dubrovnik, you said that you talked to Belgrade. Can you tell me exactly who you spoke to in Belgrade when seeking safe passage?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of Admiral Stane Brovet. I asked to speak to him, but I could not get in touch with him, so I spoke probably to the officer who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you did not talk to Admiral Brovet personally?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When your safe passage to Dubrovnik was confirmed from the office of Admiral Brovet, did you talk to General Raseta after that?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First I talked to Raseta, then Brovet. Because I wanted to get it in writing, but I never managed to, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did General Raseta also assure you verbally that you would have safe passage?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A major spoke to my wife over the telephone and said that my personal safety was guaranteed as well as safe passage in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that the only contact with General Raseta before you went to Dubrovnik? Please just wait for the question to finish. So is that the only contact in relation to safe passage? Was it only this approval given verbally that you can go to Dubrovnik? Was that the situation you refer to when you say that from Raseta's office someone called and spoke to your wife and gave a positive answer that you would have safe passage?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I talked directly to Mr. Raseta himself. And then -- well, he didn't immediately give a very clear answer. I think I actually spoke to him two or three times. But since I could not get a laissez-passer so to speak, then I called Admiral Brovet from Split. And in the evening I even asked General Mladenic and then he conveyed to me that Admiral Kandic was also giving guarantees. Everybody was giving guarantees, but unfortunately, I could not get any confirmation in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, on the 3rd of December 1991, did you ask for approval for the speedboat from the Port Authority carrying you and Cifric and Kriste, so two additional ministers, and also the representatives of the European Community, and your secretary, could travel on the 4th of December, leaving Split at 7.30, from Split to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: My secretary was not there, but it's certainly true that we asked for that. So everything you said, with the exception of the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In order to travel with the speedboat, was it Admiral Culic who gave the approval?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was not a speedboat. A speedboat is a boat that moves very fast, of course. But this one didn't really. Well, Culic is a last name from Split, but I'm not sure that that is the last name concerned in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of December, so did you take that boat, Kapetanija, in the morning at 7.00, or rather 5 minutes past 7.00? Is that when you sailed out?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was exactly 5 minutes past 7.00 in the morning, but we did leave in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you arrived in Dubrovnik on that boat, did that boat remain in Dubrovnik or was it returned immediately or the following day? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. It stayed in Dubrovnik. And it even got hit during the shelling. We returned on that same boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th, 10th -- well, five or six days later. That boat was in the harbour of Gruz, waiting for us, and it was hit during the shelling. Some glass was broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, and General Raseta, who you contacted when in Zagreb, did he belong to the 5th Military District?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. That's the Zagreb district, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you mentioned that upon arriving in Dubrovnik, the mayor of Dubrovnik familiarised you with the current situation in Dubrovnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only he, but others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which city officials spoke to you then?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were met by the president of the Assembly, Mr. Poljanic, the president of the Executive Council, Mr. Sikic. So that was the structure that prevailed in the governments in various towns then. Then we went to the city Assembly. Then Lieutenant Colonel Nojko Marinovic came. And then the negotiators were there, too, those who had negotiated with the Yugoslav People's Army; Mr. Obuljen, and another man but I cannot remember his name now. Then Mr. Simonovic was there, too. He was, I think, assistant to Mr. Nojko Marinovic then. And they all reported about the situation, about negotiations with the Yugoslav People's Army, how they had progressed, how far they got, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you had these talks at the city Assembly, and that's where you had your first meeting. Is that the building of the municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that the building in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the building in the Old Town. Where the City Cafe is, opposite the church, St. Blaise church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll have a 20-minute break now, which you will probably enjoy, Mr. Rudolf, and we will resume then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The witness is indicating there's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a moment. We will take these in order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, allow me to add to one of my previous answers to counsel's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These 20 minutes of break were quite convenient. I had a good Turkish coffee. Counsel asked me about my negotiations with the JNA. I also negotiated at the Isle of Vis with Admiral Jokic. And once again at Vis when General Raseta, Kandic, and Mladenic were present, the negotiations were led by the vice Prime Minister, deputy Prime Minister of the Croatian government, Mr. Granic, and I was attending.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me, those negotiations at the Isle of Vis when Admiral Jokic was present, did he also participate?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our first negotiations were with Admiral Kandic, who was head of the navy. And the second time, the negotiations were led by Raseta and also present were Admiral Kandic and another person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we now move to the 5th of December. You established contact with the naval sector of Boka and agreed to hold a meeting with Admiral Jokic in Cavtat. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what was the position of Admiral Jokic at that meeting of the 5th of December? What stances did he advocate on behalf of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We began with my presentation of the views of the Croatian government regarding Dubrovnik and the demands of the Croatian government that I explained in responding-in-chief. His positions were the following: He insisted that armed forces should leave Dubrovnik. He especially emphasised the mercenaries. He said that in that case, the Yugoslav People's Army would withdraw further to the east of Dubrovnik, and we discussed that at length with active participation of Mr. Risto, who is himself a local of Dubrovnik. He talked to the admiral directly. We said that if the JNA should wish to occupy Dubrovnik, there would be many casualties, there would be street fighting. Admiral Jokic gave an assessment of the armed forces, which I believe was unrealistic. He said that we were talking about 15.000 soldiers. That was his main position, and he kept repeating it. Later, we started reaching agreement about a number of details, and the first thing we agreed on was a cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We will come later to those details. Tell us again about the evaluation of Croatian forces in Dubrovnik. Did you have any information on Croatian troops, Croatian forces in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lieutenant Colonel Nojko Marinovic told me what kind of forces we had in Dubrovnik, and that number was much, much smaller, especially if we were talking about those who had real weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there any cannons, mortars, heavy weapons in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Lieutenant Colonel Nojko Marinovic tell you anything at all about whether he had any artillery at his disposal?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You made him out to be a real soldier who stood at attention when he spoke to you. Didn't he mention the status of his units, the armed forces he was in command of?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He described a situation as to where Croatian forces were deployed vis-a-vis the JNA, and frankly speaking, even if you were to tell me something about cannons and guns, I would hardly understand a word. So he did not discuss that with me. As for what you say about the impression that Lieutenant Colonel Marinovic gave me, I would say that I really believed him and that is why I described him the way I did. I wanted to say that he wouldn't have dared to tell me, a minister, something that was untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But you were supposed to lead negotiations, and weren't you supposed to get from your chief officer precise numbers of troops, artillery, weapons you had?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not discuss these details at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Apart from agreeing on a cease-fire on the 5th of December, what else did you agree with Admiral Jokic on in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We agreed that the JNA would restore water supply, electrical power, that daily services between Dubrovnik and the surrounding populated centres would be restored as well, and we even agreed on the reopening of the Dubrovnik-Split Road. The only thing we failed to reach agreement on was the question of siege or blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. I was intrigued by what you said about the restoration of local transport. Does that mean road and maritime transport equally?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreement was reached on reopening daily services between Dubrovnik and the islands and the road Dubrovnik-Split. That's the road that goes to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about Dubrovnik-Sipan?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking a lot. I don't know precisely about Sipan. But in agreement -- in principle, we reached an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, and I would like you to confirm this, what remained controversial?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of blockade remained controversial. The admiral said he was not authorised to lift the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. When you say "to lift the blockade," does that mean that naval ships would no longer be present in the coastal waters of Dubrovnik? Or does it mean something else? Could you clarify.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "naval" or maritime blockade, that means that naval vessels surround an area and do not allow ships to go through. And when you say to lift the blockade, that implies the removal of those ships that stand in the way of vessels going to Dubrovnik or from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you also explain one other thing to me: After the 7th of December, after an agreement was reached on inspection of ships in the port of Gruz, were there any naval ships remaining in that area around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean JNA ships? I don't know, to be honest. But after that, ships had no longer any difficulties sailing into Dubrovnik. After we reached that agreement, even an oil transporter set into the port of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So before the signing of this agreement, the blockade was complete. And after that, the ships going to and from Dubrovnik were inspected by the vessels of the JNA navy in the open sea?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not exactly the open sea. It's the sea outside the port of Dubrovnik. When there is a blockade, no ships can pass through, and even when we were going to Dubrovnik, we had to approach a naval vessel, an officer would come down, inspect our boat, and allow us to go on. Let me explain why it was an issue, whether the inspection would be done in the port or at sea. It was the month of December --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Allow me to interrupt you here. You already explained, talking about the Zelenika vessel. But tell me what you know about this: If the agreement envisaged inspection in the port of Gruz, does that mean that if those ships were passing at sea by naval vessels, the naval vessels did not stop them any longer, as they did before? Instead, ships would be inspected once they arrived in the port of Gruz?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That's how the inspection was done. JNA officers would go up on to the ships that had set in and inspect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So on the 5th of December, the only outstanding issue that remained was whether inspection would be done at sea or in the port of Gruz?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the issue of blockade, because I insisted that if they could lift the blockade completely, that would be the best of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So in your opinion, what does your demand to lift the blockade mean? What would that imply?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would mean the removal of naval ships blocking entry into port. After the agreement that we reached, all the other navy ships were removed and only those blocking entry into the port of Dubrovnik remained. They remained there to control inspection of incoming traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me now exactly what you agreed and what you signed. Did you agree on a complete lift of the blockade, or did you sign and implement an agreement that passenger traffic should not be controlled at sea, but instead should be controlled in the port of Gruz?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reached an agreement only on the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Regarding this control and inspection of vessels that remained controversial on the 5th of December, Admiral Jokic said that he had to consult the Supreme Command, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the negotiations, since the other issues were no longer a problem, such as the cease-fire, the reopening of roads, and the restoration of daily services, did you understand it to mean that the implementation of the agreement could start immediately?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first point was the most important to us, and I understood that we could start implementing immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And you were only awaiting for the confirmation to be received by Admiral Jokic from the Supreme Command regarding the inspection of ships?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why we agreed to meet again the next day at 10.00 in Cavtat and signed an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to show this witness Exhibit P61, tab 29, concerning Witness Hvalkof. Sorry. Just a minute, with your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, did the representatives of the European Community Monitoring Mission accompany you on the 5th of December to Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But most importantly, do you remember if they were present at the negotiations between yourself and Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure about the 7th of December, the second day, but I'm not sure about the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But tell me about the meeting of the 5th of December. After that meeting, did you inform the representative of the ECMM about the results of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Not only him, but the people of Dubrovnik and everyone concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I heard that. Please look at this exhibit of the Prosecution. It's a note written by the deputy chief of the regional centre of Dubrovnik, Mr. Per Hvalkof, to whom you referred earlier. He made a note here regarding what you conveyed to him after the meeting in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the English version could be put on the ELMO, please, so that the Trial Chamber could follow as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please look at point 3, where it says: "Mr. Rudolf said that the following subjects were discussed: (A), an unconditional cease-fire." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: "(B), reduction of the number of troops on both sides to be inspected by a joint military commission. (D), lifting the blockade of the Dubrovnik port with the JNA officers in mufti inspecting cargo in the port with a reference to the European monitors. This issue has not been resolved. Would be taken up again tomorrow." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And "(E), reopening of access roads to Dubrovnik, especially the Adriatic highway or main road." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please look at another document from P61, tab 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like that document to be shown to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, this is the letter that Admiral Jokic sent to you on the 6th of December. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We are going to go back to this letter in detail later on, but I'm interested in these proposals that he is presenting to you as the agenda for the meeting on the 7th of December, upon his return from Belgrade. Paragraph 2 says: "To accept our agreement concerning the cease-fire in the entire zone of Dubrovnik all the way up to Ston." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You already agreed to that on the 5th of December, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3: "To establish a regular shuttle between Cavtat-Dubrovnik, Zaton, Mokosica-Zaton, and twice a week from Dubrovnik to the islands." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this also agreed on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, this is a novelty in relation to what you discussed on the 5th of December. Now Admiral Jokic is proposing that ships be examined in Gruz harbour. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 says: "To open road communications from town, including the roads to Ston." Was that agreed upon on the 5th of December, too?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Adriatic road, the main Adriatic road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: He repeats under paragraph 7 his proposal to deblock the town completely and to withdraw the weapons that jeopardise the town out of shooting range and also that armed men who came to town be evacuated with the first vessel. Is that what he advocated on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is roughly his position of the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But on the 5th of December, you discussed it and no agreement was reached in terms of the withdrawal of any forces from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask that the witness be shown P162, tab 3. That is from the binder for Witness Rudolf. So P162. This is the radio log. Could the entire radio log be given to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher, actually, to place the English version on the ELMO and to put the appropriate pages as I mention them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, could you please look at page number 1, the upper left-hand corner. It starts with "The 5th of December..." The text starts with "The 5th of December..." And the page is number 1. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last time referred to on that page, 0855.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That is the message sent to the naval district. It's supposed to say "sector," though, the Boka sector. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 2 now.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It says that as regards the 6th of December, a team is mentioned, a number of persons who would be there, a sanitation expert, Gailland, and two engineers from the Dubrovnik water management company, one for machines and one for electrical installations. And on the following day, the 6th of December 1991, they would go to Komolac, inspect the pump station there. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit illegible. But yes, yes, all right. I can follow you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Further on, an explanation is given as to how this meeting would evolve in relation to the repair of the pump station in Komolac, that the regular ship line would be taken from Dubrovnik to Mokosica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you now please look at page 7 of this log, that is. The time that you're supposed to look at is 1715. It's towards the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that also a message sent to the command of VPS Boka?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. To the Boka VPS command. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It says "pursuant to the agreement signed today with representatives of the government of the Republic of Croatia, we propose that tomorrow at 0900 hours, the Arka, marked with a Red Cross flag, leave the port of Gruz with humanitarian aid for the island of Sipan with stops in the ports of Sucurac and the port of Sipan," if I manage to read this properly.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
