utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In your opinion, based on -- actually, not even so much on your opinion. You were in Dubrovnik on the 6th of December. Is it conceivable to you that the Croatian forces would have damaged their own cultural and historical monuments in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, that is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you aware of prior attacks by forces under the JNA control against the Old Town of Dubrovnik in October and November? In other words, did you know of any attacks before the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I want to say again, we always thought of Dubrovnik as a whole so that these attacks would be treated, would be thought of as attacks against Dubrovnik, including, of course, the Old Town, which is an integral part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, when I asked you whether or not you thought the Croatians may have worked damage on their own -- on cultural monuments or historical monuments in their own town or Old Town, you said it was nonsense. Can you indicate, if you know, in what esteem the people of Croatia held the Old Town of Dubrovnik? How was it viewed?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Dubrovnik, as we say, is the showcase of Croatia. It has its own history and for many centuries it used to be a republic. Croatian culture originates from that town. It is a jewel in the Republic of Croatia. And throughout the world, when you speak of Croatia, other cities are much less well known, but everybody knows of Dubrovnik. On the day when Dubrovnik was attacked, on the 6th, I got telephone calls from Italy, from London, protests were made from everywhere, from all over the world over that attack. Politically speaking, to attack Dubrovnik is something that is inconceivable to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were asked during cross-examination if you specifically mentioned when you spoke with Admiral Jokic about the Old Town, and your response - I'd have to pull the page - was that you included it within the bigger framework of Dubrovnik. Do you recall giving -- do you recall -- would it help if you took a look at your statement when you were asked about what you relayed concerning the Old Town to Admiral Jokic? Would it assist you to recall what you may have said to the Office of the Prosecutor at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning. This question was asked and clearly answered, both in-chief and in cross-examination. I don't know what my learned friend is expecting to happen now. Does she mean to correct the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination? Or does she want to distance herself from the witness's answers? I believe this line of questioning is inadmissible in every way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the purpose of examination is not to trick a witness. If he has given some response and he is perhaps not recollecting it, and if it would assist to refresh recollection, this would be the appropriate vehicle in which to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The problem is it's not a case of inability to recall; the question has been asked and answered. I must say I agree with Mr. Petrovic at the present time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The location of the Hotel Argentina gave you a view of the -- part of the Old Town. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And when you were speaking about the shelling of Dubrovnik on the telephone, both to the assistant to Admiral Jokic and to the admiral, did you indicate the intensity with which the shelling was happening? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said to him that Dubrovnik was being shelled. You see, from the Hotel Argentina you can see the Old Town, as it is usually shown by all photographs and cards. We could see that it was being shelled. That was not at issue. I wrote in my letter to General Strugar that the Old Town was being shelled. Whether I drew attention to the Old Town in particular in that telephone conversation, I'm not sure. We could see that the other part of Dubrovnik behind us was being shelled, but we could see that the Old Town was being shelled. I don't think it was at issue. It was a terrible sight when those buildings were on fire. And you could clearly see the fire coming from inside the ramparts. And the next day, the sight was horrible in the Old Town itself. Heaven forbid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did either Admiral Jokic, if you recall, or his assistant or anyone else you may have spoken to from the JNA that day ask you the condition of the Old Town? Do you recall if a question emanated or originated from the JNA side once you indicated that Dubrovnik was under attack?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. But what I said to Admiral Jokic, that an attack against Dubrovnik was under way, he must have known what Dubrovnik looked like, and he must have known that we were in Hotel Argentina. It must have been clear that the whole town was being shelled, including the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection about any conversations you may have had with Admiral Jokic or his assistants at any point concerning the -- ultimately concerning the Old Town, irrespective of the time? Did you mention anything that day in your direct dealings with either of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object. Your Honour, this question was just asked a minute ago. This is just a different phrasing used by my learned friend to try to get an answer she wants to hear. This question was asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It has a wider scope. It's irrespective of time, Mr. Petrovic. Carry on, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, did you understand my question or shall I repeat it? My question was do you have any recollection about any conversations you may have had --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. When we met up again the next day -- you see, it's very difficult to recount these details with any degree of certainty after so much time. But I don't know if it is at issue at all that the Old Town was attacked, was shelled. Is there any doubt?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever receive from General Strugar prior to the telex, or anybody acting on General Strugar's behalf, any concern expressed for the protection of the Old Town from the time of the shelling's beginning? Did anyone from the JNA side ask how the Old Town was faring, whether it was -- whether there was any activity happening? Was there any inquiry affirmatively made by anybody from the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the JNA side, no. I didn't mention General Strugar because he didn't matter to me. Admiral Jokic mattered to me because I negotiated with him as representative of the Yugoslav People's Army. And when I said those two ships were being attacked, those ships at the time were located under the ramparts of the Old Town. Admiral Jokic knew the layout of Dubrovnik better than I did, and everyone in the army knew what the city looked like. And when shelling started, it's logical that shells fell everywhere. I don't know if it -- there is any controversy as to the shelling of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say the ships, are you referring to the ships -- the Argosy, the one you call the parliament or parliamentarian ships?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, these two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And these ships were in the old port harbour of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's called the City Port. It's right in front of the ramparts. There are two entrances into Dubrovnik, and they were berthed in right next to the walls.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In plain view to all who were above the city looking at the city and the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will take the liberty of suggesting to the President of the Trial Chamber and the Judges: Go to Dubrovnik. There is this hill of Zarkovica and another hill, Bosanka. When you go up, Dubrovnik is like in the palm of your hand. You can throw an apple down. The first thing I did when Dubrovnik was liberated was to go up that hill to get a view of Dubrovnik. If you ever have the opportunity, I beg you, please go up there and see. You can reach the top of the hill by car. From the hotel, we couldn't leave. We couldn't go out into the street because we were directly under fire from the Zarkovica hill, from Bosanka, and the Srdj Hill, which is in the middle between the two. And then you will have an exact precise impression of what it was all like. When I watched the shelling, it looked like the shells were falling and destroying the town. It was like Goliath was throwing some sort of weapons on the town and destroying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect your answer was yes. And we may have to take you up on your suggestion at some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just one or two very quick points since our time is up, if the Chamber will indulge me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The correction that was referred to about Mr. Mihocevic. You made a correction, and was that only as to the spelling of his name? Instead of Mico, you wanted it to be Miso? Nothing about titles, is that correct, or rank? Thank you. And you were asked -- there was a reference during cross-examination about the party who was representing the JNA or the Supreme Command for signature on the 7th. Was it your expectation that it would still be Admiral Jokic as he was the person who you met with on the 5th and had indicated that he was there and apologised through General Strugar? Did you expect Admiral Jokic to be there on the 7th as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where, in town?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you expect Admiral Jokic to be the person signing on behalf of the Supreme Command on the 7th given that he was the person you had been dealing with on the 5th for the initial set of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I expected Admiral Jokic to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of time, I will --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Rudolf, did you want to say something else?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just this: I didn't invite the general to come to Dubrovnik. I invited Mr. Strugar to come to Dubrovnik and see. He is a well-educated man, a soldier. He would have seen for himself because Mr. Strugar sent me that radiogram, and I thought it would have been a good idea for him to come and see for himself what had happened. But no, I did not invite Jokic. I didn't call him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just to correct the record. You said that "I did not invite the general to come to Dubrovnik, I invited Mr. Strugar." When you said "general," were you again referring to the admiral? The terms seem to get confused in the record. Okay.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the admiral. It's the kind of mistake that those of us who are not soldiers tend to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just to confirm, that despite your having been informed that General Strugar would be your negotiating partner, you were told by Admiral Jokic that he would be handling it on behalf of General Strugar, were you at all surprised --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. That is not in evidence. That has not been said. Would my learned friend kindly say where it was said, on which page in the wording that she seems to be putting into her question. What she is doing now is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's the "on behalf of General Strugar." We had this earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Rather than General Strugar. Rather than General Strugar, despite what you were told in Zagreb, were you -- was it expected by you that you would continue to deal with Admiral Jokic as the representative for these negotiations, negotiations of the 5th and what would have been the 6th but ended up being the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat again: I was told in Zagreb and I was told from Belgrade that I would be negotiating with General Strugar. When I got in touch with this liaison officer - what's his name - Jeremic, he told me first that Jokic would be coming. When the negotiations started, Admiral Jokic only said that General Strugar would not be coming, and that he would be negotiating on behalf of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the SFRY, that is, Yugoslavia, that he was authorised to negotiate. That was sufficient to us. As I told you, I didn't care. It was a matter of indifference to us who it would be; Kadijevic or anyone else. What mattered was that it be a representative of the general staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your post, your position as minister of maritime affairs, would you have expected to have been informed if, in fact, any action on the 6th of December from the sea were implicated? Would you, as the minister of maritime affairs, expect to have been made aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. As a matter of fact, I was a bit surprised to hear it is the Navy only that took part in the attack. If that suits you, then prove it. I was a bit surprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you ever informed that -- sorry. Your own observations to confirm --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, for the extra time. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We must draw to an end very quickly. Two things. To you Ms. Somers: Looking ahead, the Chamber was surprised to see that for the last two witnesses you have contemplated eight hours examination-in-chief for each. There are very detailed expert reports from each. We would invite you to consider whether you need anything like that time for examination-in-chief. The second and important thing, Mr. -- or Dr. Rudolf, is to thank you indeed for your patience. We gave you a very interrupted time earlier. We apologise again for that. We thank you for your attendance and what you have done to help us. And we wish you a safe journey home. We will adjourn now for the evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I took advantage of this weekend, don't you worry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We had confidence in your initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
